column4: The section’s dictionary form of ب ل و means testing; this ayah explicitly says both harm and good are a fitnah, so abundance and constriction can each be a trial rather than a rank.
The section’s dictionary root ب ل و is used here for testing a people by good things and bad things, making the two-sided trial in 89:15 concrete in a historical community.
The ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و for testing people through what God has given them and says they differ in rank; this separates entrusted gifts from earned standing.

The ayah says some people are made a trial for others and asks whether they will be patient; it makes the section’s meeting of the well-provided person and the vulnerable orphan a test of how people treat each other.
The section cites this correction to a person who attributes a gift to his own knowledge: the ayah calls the granted blessing a fitnah, directly reversing the reading of provision as proof of merit.

After Qarun is swallowed by the earth, those who had wanted his place recognize that God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it; this gives the section’s correction a scene of repentant witnesses.

The ayah says provision would lead people to transgress if expanded without limit, so God sends it down by measure; the section’s dictionary root ق د ر names this limit as measured provision rather than contempt.
The command not to fix one’s gaze on others’ worldly adornment says it is a test; this directly checks the section’s human inference that visible ease proves divine honor.
The ayah calls wealth and children a fitnah; this specifically connects the section’s provision and family-care images to what can test a person.
Like the section’s account of blessing as a trial, this ayah names wealth and children themselves as a fitnah, making care and resources responsibilities as well as gifts.
The ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و for testing who does best in deeds through the earth’s adornment; it shifts attention from possessing comfort to what a person does with it.

This ayah specifies the wealth and children being extended; 23:56 supplies the question whether these mean good is being hastened, making the gifts themselves the section’s test rather than proof of honor.
This continuation answers the question in 23:55: those gifts are not proof that good is being hastened to their owners, completing the section’s reversal of wealth as rank.
The affluent claim that greater wealth and children mean they will not be punished; their boast is a direct instance of reading provision as honor, which the section challenges.
The ayah answers the boast in 34:35 by saying God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it with the section’s root ق د ر; distribution, not human status, controls the scene.
The ayah completes 34:35 and 34:36 by saying wealth and children do not bring people near to God; it draws the boundary between worldly means and actual standing.

For a person whose provision is restricted, the ayah commands spending from what God has given; it repeats the section’s wording from the root ق د ر and connects constriction with care measured to one’s means.
The ayah says God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it; it uses the section’s root ق د ر for this change, rather than validating the claim “my Lord has humiliated me.”
This ayah names the father-and-son scene in 37:102 a clear trial, making explicit that a family bond, too, can be the setting of ibtilāʾ.
The section’s dictionary branch for ر ب ب names a wife’s son as a rabīb, and its branch for ح ج ر names the lap; this ayah joins “stepdaughters” with “in your laps” in one family ruling.
The section’s dictionary branch for ر ب ب describes raising someone through stages; the adult’s prayer remembers that his parents raised him صغيرًا and asks God to show them mercy in return.
Pharaoh asks Moses whether he was not raised among them as a child; the section cites this use of ر ب ب to show human upbringing being invoked as a claim over the grown child.
God tells Moses’ mother to nurse him and, when afraid, place him in the river without fear; the infant-care scene makes the section’s picture of a child nourished and protected tangible.
After 28:11’s watch, Moses’ sister offers to direct the household to someone who will care for him when he refuses other nurses; it continues the infant-care scene.
The ayah says Moses was returned to his mother so she would be comforted and not grieve; it completes the caregiving scene of 28:7 and gives reunion its own contribution.
The ayah recalls a mother carrying her child through weakness and nursing him for two years, then commands gratitude to parents; it supplies the bodily care behind the section’s family image.
The ayah remembers a mother’s hardship in carrying and bearing a child and marks his growth to maturity; it makes the section’s child-reared-through-stages image explicit.
The ayah recalls that God found the Prophet an orphan and gave him shelter; the section’s principle that one who was sheltered should shelter others is grounded in this personal history.
This neighboring grace recalls the Prophet’s need and God’s provision for him; beside the orphan-shelter memory in 93:6 and the command in 93:9, it links received care to later responsibility.
The ayah directly commands that the orphan not be oppressed; after the Prophet’s own shelter in 93:6, it turns care received into care owed.

The ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و to say to test orphans until marriageable age, then hand them their property and avoid consuming it hastily; it joins trial, childhood, delayed care, and a guardian’s duty.
Asked about orphans, the ayah says setting their affairs right is best and calls them brothers; it directly answers the section’s account of the orphan’s care being neglected or delayed.
The ayah commands that orphans receive their property and forbids replacing or consuming it; this names a concrete opposite to ikram as active care.
When inheritance is divided, the ayah directs that orphans and the poor who are present receive something and kind words; it makes the orphan’s claim visible at a moment of wealth distribution.
The ayah forbids approaching an orphan’s property except in the best way until maturity; it protects the child’s resources while he remains too young to manage them.
The ayah repeats the duty to guard an orphan’s property in the best manner until maturity; it makes sustained protection, rather than possession by the guardian, the measure of care.
Moses and his companion preserve treasure for two orphan boys until they grow up; this is a particular scene of a child’s future being protected when his father is absent.
The ayah warns that those who consume orphan property unjustly consume fire; it marks a specific boundary opposite the section’s call to honor the orphan.
The ayah commands giving the orphan his due; it turns the section’s shift from claiming one’s own honor to performing an obligation for someone else into a material act.
The ayah makes spending beloved wealth on orphans part of righteousness; this joins the section’s definition of ك ر م as generosity with the orphan who needs it.
The righteous feed the orphan, the poor, and the captive despite loving the food themselves; this is a direct act of generous care rather than a claim to status.
This ayah identifies a near-relative orphan; 90:14 supplies feeding during severe hunger, joining kinship and orphanhood in the section’s family-care scene.
The ayah says the denier pushes the orphan away; this gives a concrete scene for the section’s dictionary explanation that the orphan is neglected.
The ayah assigns a share of communal wealth to orphans and other vulnerable groups so wealth will not circulate only among the rich; it directly counters using abundance as a private rank.
The section cites the ayah’s use of أكرمكم: the most honored before God is the most God-conscious, not the person with the most provision.
In Hell the boastful offender is taunted as “mighty, noble”; the ironic use of ك ر ي م reverses the section’s question of what genuine honor means.

The ayah says people rejoice in worldly life while its enjoyment is only brief, alongside God’s extending and restricting provision with the section’s root ق د ر; it loosens the link between a large share and lasting honor.
The ayah repeats that God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it, using the section’s root ق د ر and reinforcing that variation in provision does not itself rank its recipient.
The ayah asks people to notice that God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it with the section’s root ق د ر; this directly counters judging honor by material ease.

The ayah asks whether people know God expands and restricts provision at will, using the section’s root ق د ر; it supports the distinction between divine distribution and the human verdict of being honored or despised.
Qarun says he was given his wealth because of knowledge he possessed; this is the same self-attribution of abundance that the section sets against God’s will in 28:82.

This ayah stages Abraham’s command to his son and the son’s response; 37:106 names the scene a clear trial, connecting the section’s test image to family attachment without confusing it with prosperity.
This neighboring command tells children to show kindness to parents in old age; 17:24 supplies the reason in its own contribution, remembering how they raised the child when small.
Pharaoh’s next line accuses Moses of a past deed after claiming to have raised him in 26:18; this shows how care can be wielded as leverage by a powerful guardian.

The Egyptian asks his wife to honor Joseph’s lodging and considers taking him as a son; this makes the section’s foster-child sense of ر ب ب and its account of ك ر م as an act toward another concrete.
This ayah continues 28:7 by having Moses’ sister watch the infant from a distance after he is placed in the river; it contributes the family’s protective follow-up.
Moses recounts being returned to his mother so she could be comforted and not grieve; this repeated account joins the section’s image of nurture to the relief of a parent.
The ayah conditions marriage to orphan girls on fear of acting justly toward them; its own context makes fairness to a vulnerable child the test, rather than treating her as an available possession.
The ayah addresses orphan girls whose prescribed rights are withheld; it names a concrete form of the neglect that the section’s dictionary branch of ي ت م associates with the orphan.
Asked what to spend, the ayah lists orphans among those to whom resources go; it makes the section’s care an allocation of provision, not a self-description.
This ayah after 107:2 says he does not urge feeding the poor; it continues the rebuke from rejecting the orphan to withholding encouragement for material care.
Israel’s covenant includes doing good to orphans; it makes care for them a standing communal duty, alongside family and the poor.
The ayah commands good treatment of orphans alongside parents, relatives, and other vulnerable neighbors; it extends the section’s family scene into social conduct.
Orphans have a named share in the distribution of war gains; this gives the section’s call to honor them a concrete communal provision.

The ayah says communities are tested in what they have been given and immediately tells them to race toward good works; it joins the section’s trial-by-provision image to its dictionary definition of generosity as outdoing another.
The command to compete in good works gives a Quranic form to the section’s dictionary definition of ك ر م as outdoing another in generosity, turning competition toward deeds.
The ayah says God exalts and humbles whom He wills; it distinguishes actual divine elevation from the human assumption that reduced provision means being despised.
The section cites the wording that whoever God humiliates has no one to honor him; this sets true divine judgment apart from a person merely inferring humiliation from scarcity.

The command not to drive away those who call on God morning and evening stages a direct rejection of the socially lowly; 6:53 explains that people are tested through one another and asks whether these are the ones God favored.

This ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و for people being tested by one another, then voices the status question “Are these whom God favored?”; it directly exposes the same false reading of provision that the section corrects.
The ayah asks guardians to imagine leaving weak children behind in the context of orphan property; 4:10 names the consequence of consuming that property, making the orphan’s vulnerability familial.

The ayah details nursing a child, the father’s duty to provide and clothe, and the parents’ shared decision about weaning; it makes the section’s image of a child raised and sustained through care concrete.
After 76:8 depicts feeding the orphan, poor, and captive, this ayah says the feeders seek no repayment or thanks; it makes care an act toward the vulnerable rather than a claim to honor.
This ayah names feeding during severe hunger; 90:15 specifies an orphan of near kin, so the cited detail places material care inside the section’s family image.
The ayah calls wealth and children worldly adornment but says lasting good deeds are better; it sets the section’s perceived signs of honor against durable conduct.
The ayah names mutual boasting and competition in increasing wealth and children as features of worldly life; this directly parallels the section’s mistaken use of abundance as rank.
The command not to be impressed by a people’s wealth and children directly reverses the section’s claim that abundance proves a person honored.
This ayah repeats the command not to be impressed by wealth and children; its repeated reversal reinforces the section’s warning against treating visible provision as rank.
The ayah forbids killing children for fear of poverty and says God provides for both parent and child; it makes scarcity a boundary against withholding care from a child.
This ayah identifies the blind man who came in the scene begun by 80:1; it gives a concrete vulnerable petitioner whose arrival is met with neglect.
The ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و for testing and names loss of wealth among its trials; it gives a specific form of constriction that the section says should not be read as humiliation.
The ayah says people will be tested in wealth and selves; it reinforces the section’s account of material fortune as a trial, while its own context adds injury and hardship.

The ayah says God expands or restricts provision for whom He wills and places the keys of heaven and earth under His authority; it repeats the section’s root ق د ر while grounding provision in divine rule.

The ayah says one does not attain birr until giving from what one loves; the section’s dictionary branch for ي ت م says the orphan is neglected in his birr, and this ayah makes that goodness depend on costly giving.

The ayah distinguishes those who spent before victory from those who spent later while promising good to both; it gives a concrete Quranic scene for the section’s dictionary image of outdoing another in generosity.
The command to remain with those who call on God and not turn one’s gaze away toward worldly adornment draws a specific boundary against preferring visible status over humble people.
Following the command not to oppress the orphan in 93:9, this ayah says not to rebuff the asker; it extends the section’s care ethic to another vulnerable petitioner.
This ayah identifies the poor person in the same feeding passage as 90:14 and 90:15; it extends that passage’s concrete care from the near-relative orphan to a destitute person.
The ayah opens with turning away; 80:2 identifies the arriving blind man, making this a specific scene of the neglect the section’s dictionary note associates with the orphan.
This ayah introduces the person who considers himself self-sufficient; 80:6 shows attention being directed to him, a specific social-status contrast to neglecting the orphan.
This ayah shows the speaker devoting attention to the self-sufficient man introduced in 80:5; 80:8 and 80:10 describe attention diverted from the striver, exposing status-based regard.
This ayah introduces the person who comes striving; 80:10 says attention is diverted from him, a concrete parallel to the section’s neglected orphan.
This ayah says the striver of 80:8 comes in fear of God; 80:10 then describes turning away from him, sharpening the contrast between moral worth and received attention.
This ayah says attention is diverted from the striving petitioner introduced in 80:8; it completes the scene of overlooking the vulnerable while attending to the self-sufficient man in 80:5 and 80:6.
